title: VLANs: Several Networks on One Switch
oneLiner: Split one physical switch into separate networks for office, production and guests, carry them all on one cable with tags, and route between them under firewall rules.
keyTakeaway: A VLAN (virtual LAN) makes a group of switch ports behave as its own separate network: its own broadcast domain and usually its own subnet. Devices in different VLANs can only talk through a router, which is exactly where you put the rules about who may talk to whom.
explanation:
Without VLANs, every device plugged into a switch is on the same network: the same broadcasts, the same subnet, and nothing stopping an office laptop from reaching a PLC. Buying separate switches for every group works but wastes hardware and cabling. A VLAN does it in configuration: each access port (a port for one ordinary device) is assigned to a VLAN, and the switch keeps frames from different VLANs apart as if they were on different switches.

To carry several VLANs over one cable, between switches or up to a router, a trunk port adds a small tag to each frame. The standard is IEEE 802.1Q: 4 extra bytes holding a 12-bit VLAN ID, so IDs run from 1 to 4094, plus 3 priority bits used for Quality of Service (QoS, putting voice or control traffic first). Devices on access ports never see the tags; the switch adds them going onto a trunk and removes them coming off.

Since each VLAN is its own subnet, traffic between VLANs has to be routed. A router with one trunk to the switch (router on a stick) or a Layer 3 switch does it, and that's the place for access rules: the office may open the HMI's web page, production may upload to the historian, guests may only reach the internet. This is segmentation, the basic tool for limiting how far an attack or a misbehaving device can spread, and the foundation of plant network security (see OT/ICS Security).
